biology.physicalDescription: Large felid with muscular body, round head, and powerful jaws. Coat orange with black stripes; white on belly, chest, and inner limbs. Tail long with black rings and black tip.
biology.behaviour: Solitary and territorial. Primarily nocturnal. Excellent swimmer — unlike most cats, tigers readily enter water. Communicates through vocalizations (roars, chuffs), scent marking, and scratch marks.
biology.communication: Roaring (long-distance), chuffing (friendly), growling/hissing (aggression). Scent marking with urine and gland secretions. Visual signals via scratch marks.
biology.reproduction: No fixed breeding season. Gestation 93-112 days. Litter size 2-4 cubs. Cubs dependent on mother for 18-24 months.
biology.lifeCycle: Born blind and helpless. Eyes open at 6-14 days. Weaned at 3-6 months. Learn hunting from mother. Dispersal at 18-24 months. Sexual maturity at 3-4 years (females), 4-5 years (males).

habitat: Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests
ecology.diet: Obligate carnivore. Prefers large ungulates: chital, sambar, gaur, wild pig. Also takes smaller prey: porcupines, hares, peafowl. Scavenges when opportunity arises.
ecology.feedingBehaviour: Stalk and ambush predator. Kills by throat bite (large prey) or nape bite (small prey). Drags kill to cover. Consumes 18-40 kg per meal.
ecology.ecologicalRole: Apex predator. Regulates herbivore populations, maintaining forest structure and biodiversity. Umbrella species — protecting tigers protects entire ecosystems.
adaptations: Striped camouflage in dappled forest light
Powerful forelimbs for grappling large prey
Swimming ability for crossing rivers and cooling

importance.ecologicalImportance: Apex predator maintaining trophic cascades. Protects forest carbon stocks and water security across range.
importance.economicImportance: Major driver of wildlife tourism in India, Nepal, Bangladesh. Tiger reserves generate significant revenue.
importance.scientificImportance: Model species for conservation biology, population genetics, landscape ecology.
importance.culturalImportance: National animal of India and Bangladesh. Deep cultural and religious significance in Hindu mythology (vehicle of Durga). Featured on currency, emblems.
importance.educationalImportance: Flagship species for conservation education globally.

biology.behaviour: Highly adaptable, opportunistic. Solitary hunter but social in family groups. Territorial. Caches food. Excellent hearing (low-frequency) for locating rodents under snow/soil. Mostly crepuscular/nocturnal.
biology.communication: Vocalizations: barks, screams, howls, 'gekkering'. Scent marking: urine, feces, anal gland. Body language: ear/tail position.
biology.reproduction: Monogamous pair bonds. Breeding season winter (Jan-Mar). Gestation 51-53 days. Litter 4-6 kits (up to 13). Both parents care for young. Kits disperse at 6-8 months.

ecology.diet: Opportunistic omnivore. Small mammals (rodents, rabbits), birds, insects, fruits, berries, carrion, human refuse. Diet varies seasonally and regionally.

adaptations: Acute low-frequency hearing for rodent detection

importance.economicImportance: Fur trade (historical). Pest control (rodents). Poultry predation (conflict).
importance.agriculturalImportance: Beneficial rodent control in farms. Minor poultry losses.
importance.medicalImportance: Rabies vector in some regions. Echinococcus multilocularis host.
importance.scientificImportance: Model for urban adaptation, behavioral ecology, range expansion.
importance.culturalImportance: Folklore worldwide: trickster figure. 'Fox' in language metaphors. Hunted for sport (UK, historically).
importance.educationalImportance: Accessible urban wildlife for public engagement.
